Article continues below this ad
The measure would permit the state to loan middle-income residents up to 17% of the cost of newly constructed houses, townhomes, row houses, condominiums and manufactured homes. Families with a traditional mortgage would only have to put 3% down.
Under Prop 37 in San Francisco, a family would need $40,000 for a median-priced home of about $1.3 million — compared to a 20% down payment of about $267,000.
Californians are clamoring for down payment help. When the state launched a down payment assistance program for first-time homebuyers in 2023, the $300 million on offer was spoken for in less than two weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/california-home-buyer-assistance-program-17888975.php).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But Prop 37 takes a different tack than traditional efforts like that one.
To start, it wouldn’t cost taxpayers a dime (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop37-110326.pdf).
The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds — which would be repaid by homeowners’ monthly loan and interest payments, not by taxpayers. Loan payments would also cover the administrative costs of the program, which will undergo an annual independent audit.
Nor will the measure drive up housing prices by subsidizing demand.
Only new homes explicitly constructed under the rules of the measure are eligible for Prop 37 loans. This incentivizes development instead of simply allowing more buyers to compete for a limited supply of existing homes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 37 aims to juice construction by eliminating red tape, particularly for condos.
Although condos are often the most affordable option for would-be homeowners, their production has fallen dramatically in California due to the state’s “right to repair” law, which effectively encourages homeowners to sue developers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/condo-home-california-law-22306098.php) for alleged construction defects — even easily fixable ones that aren’t harmful.
This year, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, attempted a fix with a bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1903) that would have comprehensively overhauled California’s right-to-repair law.
But it died in the final moments of the legislative session (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTA2MTM0fDc4YTAyODgwNzMxZGY1NThiZTI5MGVlZGUxOTA2Y2VhYzNlNTFlMGM3YTJkYTNhNjZiNzFhZTljYzM1Njg5ODM&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=Is%20Gavin%20Newsom%20in%20his%20lame%20duck%20era%3F&utm_campaign=WhatMatters) — even after being significantly watered down.
Prop 37 would reanimate some aspects of Wicks’ bill.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It would require claimants to clearly specify each alleged violation and permit them to release builders from liability if repairs are completed satisfactorily. It also incentivizes quick resolution of lawsuits — builders could ask courts to dismiss actions against them if claimants drag their feet — and caps attorneys’ fees at 30% of total recovery.
With legislative reform in limbo, “the condo defect implications of Prop 37 are solid,” Leora Tanjuatco Ross, YIMBY Action’s California director, told the editorial board.
We certainly hope that lawmakers pursue more transformative defect reform in the future. But until that happens, Prop 37 could serve as a stopgap.
The ability of middle-class buyers to finance a home, such as these along Kirkwood Avenue in San Francisco, seen on April 9, 2022, would be enhanced with the passage of S.F.’s Prop 37 in November.
Justin Katigbak/For the S.F. Chronicle The measure also requires builders who want to take advantage of these right-to-repair reforms to meet certain labor standards, such as providing workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance, while abiding by state and local laws requiring prevailing wage — or union-level pay — for large-scale projects.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Those who have lived in California for at least a year and have a family income of 80% to 200% of the area median income — which in San Francisco ranges from about $104,000 to $260,000 for a family of two (https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/2026_AMI-IncomeLimits-HMFA.pdf) — are eligible for Prop 37 loans.
No, you can’t use Prop 37 for a second home; qualifying homes must be the buyer’s primary residence. Eligible home prices are capped, too — they can’t be sold for more than 125% of the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in the county in question, which is about $1.5 million in San Francisco.
The measure also contains consumer protections. For instance, it requires the program’s mortgage loans to be fixed-rate and instructs the California Housing Finance Agency to set them “as low as possible.” It also permits the agency to establish a homeowner education requirement.
Just how affordable these loans would be, however, is an open question. As a California Budget Center analysis noted (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/#h-how-is-prop-37-different-from-california-s-existing-downpayment-assistance-programs), the Housing Finance Agency’s loans may come with higher-than-usual interest rates because they’re second mortgages. Investors view these as riskier than first mortgages, which are repaid first if a homeowner defaults.
Former state Sen. Bob Hertzberg, a Democrat from Los Angeles County who collected signatures to put Prop 37 on the ballot, told the editorial board that he believes the measure could create 190,000 homes and spur $150 billion in economic activity.
That certainly sounds transformative. But is the measure likely to live up to Hertzberg’s hype?
Prop 37 has no formal opposition and most experts we spoke with were cautiously supportive.
The measure technically didn’t need to go to the ballot; the Legislature or housing finance agency could have established the program. We’re not a fan of politicians using the ballot for their vanity projects, and there’s certainly some ego at play for Hertzberg, who referred to the homes that could be built under Prop 37 as “Hertzberg houses.”
But Hertzberg did try to get the Legislature to approve a version of the program (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/sites/shou.senate.ca.gov/files/7.%20SB%201457%20%28Hertzberg%29%20-%20analysis.pdf), to no avail.
“I’m just a burnt-out old politician trying to do the right thing who hasn’t lost his soul, and I might help the motherf—ers in the middle class if I die doing it,” said Hertzberg, who clearly subscribes to the John Burton school of profanity. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/john-burton-obituary-17820175.php)

Prop 37’s scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change California’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
We recommend a yes vote.

That down payment amount is based on the statewide median $900,000 price tag for a house, according to recent data from (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/sept2026sales) the California Assn. of Realtors. In Los Angeles County, the median price for a single-family home is $935,000. In Orange County, it’s $1.5 million.
Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households. For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state’s existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.

The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
“Prop. 37 is a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families — at zero cost or risk to taxpayers,” Newsom said in a statement.

But Proposition 37 carries a significant caveat: Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building, some critics said.
Also, the proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure is approved. And some have questioned whether there will be sufficiently robust interest from investors to buy the state-issued bonds that will be used to fund the down payment loans.
The concept of down payment assistance is not new. Cities and states, including California, have long offered such programs to low- and middle-income homeowners, either in the form of loans or grants, and there are reportedly more than 2,700 such programs (https://downpaymentresource.com/professional-resource/down-payment-assistance-continues-to-expand-in-q1-2026-reaching-2679-programs-nationwide/) across the country.
Nevada, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York all have programs to help homebuyers afford a down payment. Since 2021, New York has dispersed $70 million (https://www.ncsha.org/hfa-news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-major-milestones-in-expanding-access-to-affordable-homeownership/) in down payment assistance. In Massachusetts, more than $146 million has been doled out in down payment help to homebuyers since 2020.
How the program would work
Under Proposition 37, down payment loans would work like any other, and would carry an interest rate and payback period — all of which would be determined by the California Housing Finance Agency.
To qualify, borrowers would need to have lived in the state for at least a year and earn no more than 200% of the local median income; in Los Angeles County, for example, that equates to a family of four earning no more than $216,200 a year.

Prop 37 endorsement: Buying a home in California can feel impossible. Is this the fix?
Most down-payment assistance programs for home buyers drive up housing costs. Prop 37 is different.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 15, 2026
It’s no secret that buying a home in California is a grim and mostly futile undertaking.
In the Bay Area, you need to make about $444,000 a year just to purchase a mid-priced home, according to a May report from the real estate brokerage Redfin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/home-buy-income-bay-area-22281201.php). A 2025 Zillow study found (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/mortgage-rate-bay-area-20792146.php) that even if mortgage rates fell to 0%, most Bay Area families still couldn’t comfortably afford to buy.
Statewide, the median home price hovers around $900,000, according to the California Association of Realtors (https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=9NSXc_YN30g). That puts a traditional 20% down payment out of reach for many families, locking them out of a pathway to generational wealth while simultaneously reducing the state’s political muscle as residents flee (https://www.ppic.org/blog/whos-leaving-california-and-whos-moving-in/) to cheaper, primarily red (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/housing-development-california-state-21027403.php), states.
Proposition 37 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot promises to help solve these problems by making it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership.

The measure would permit the state to loan middle-income residents up to 17% of the cost of newly constructed houses, townhomes, row houses, condominiums and manufactured homes. Families with a traditional mortgage would only have to put 3% down.
Under Prop 37 in San Francisco, a family would need $40,000 for a median-priced home of about $1.3 million — compared to a 20% down payment of about $267,000.
Californians are clamoring for down payment help. When the state launched a down payment assistance program for first-time homebuyers in 2023, the $300 million on offer was spoken for in less than two weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/california-home-buyer-assistance-program-17888975.php).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But Prop 37 takes a different tack than traditional efforts like that one.
To start, it wouldn’t cost taxpayers a dime (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop37-110326.pdf).
The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds — which would be repaid by homeowners’ monthly loan and interest payments, not by taxpayers. Loan payments would also cover the administrative costs of the program, which will undergo an annual independent audit.
Nor will the measure drive up housing prices by subsidizing demand.
Only new homes explicitly constructed under the rules of the measure are eligible for Prop 37 loans. This incentivizes development instead of simply allowing more buyers to compete for a limited supply of existing homes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 37 aims to juice construction by eliminating red tape, particularly for condos.
Although condos are often the most affordable option for would-be homeowners, their production has fallen dramatically in California due to the state’s “right to repair” law, which effectively encourages homeowners to sue developers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/condo-home-california-law-22306098.php) for alleged construction defects — even easily fixable ones that aren’t harmful.
This year, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, attempted a fix with a bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1903) that would have comprehensively overhauled California’s right-to-repair law.

It also incentivizes quick resolution of lawsuits — builders could ask courts to dismiss actions against them if claimants drag their feet — and caps attorneys’ fees at 30% of total recovery.
With legislative reform in limbo, “the condo defect implications of Prop 37 are solid,” Leora Tanjuatco Ross, YIMBY Action’s California director, told the editorial board.

Those who have lived in California for at least a year and have a family income of 80% to 200% of the area median income — which in San Francisco ranges from about $104,000 to $260,000 for a family of two (https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/2026_AMI-IncomeLimits-HMFA.pdf) — are eligible for Prop 37 loans.

Eligible home prices are capped, too — they can’t be sold for more than 125% of the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in the county in question, which is about $1.5 million in San Francisco.

A 2025 Zillow study found (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/mortgage-rate-bay-area-20792146.php) that even if mortgage rates fell to 0%, most Bay Area families still couldn’t comfortably afford to buy.
Statewide, the median home price hovers around $900,000, according to the California Association of Realtors (https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=9NSXc_YN30g). Proposition 37 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot promises to help solve these problems by making it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Buying a home in California requires a colossal amount of money — and coming up with a 20% cash down payment of $180,000 for a median price home is a staggering hurdle for many would-be buyers.
That down payment amount is based on the statewide median $900,000 price tag for a house, according to recent data from (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/sept2026sales) the California Assn. of Realtors. In Los Angeles County, the median price for a single-family home is $935,000. In Orange County, it’s $1.5 million.
Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households. For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state’s existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.

The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
“Prop. 37 is a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families — at zero cost or risk to taxpayers,” Newsom said in a statement.

But Proposition 37 carries a significant caveat: Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building, some critics said.
Also, the proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure is approved. And some have questioned whether there will be sufficiently robust interest from investors to buy the state-issued bonds that will be used to fund the down payment loans.
The concept of down payment assistance is not new. Cities and states, including California, have long offered such programs to low- and middle-income homeowners, either in the form of loans or grants, and there are reportedly more than 2,700 such programs (https://downpaymentresource.com/professional-resource/down-payment-assistance-continues-to-expand-in-q1-2026-reaching-2679-programs-nationwide/) across the country.
Nevada, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York all have programs to help homebuyers afford a down payment. Since 2021, New York has dispersed $70 million (https://www.ncsha.org/hfa-news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-major-milestones-in-expanding-access-to-affordable-homeownership/) in down payment assistance. In Massachusetts, more than $146 million has been doled out in down payment help to homebuyers since 2020.
How the program would work
Under Proposition 37, down payment loans would work like any other, and would carry an interest rate and payback period — all of which would be determined by the California Housing Finance Agency.
To qualify, borrowers would need to have lived in the state for at least a year and earn no more than 200% of the local median income; in Los Angeles County, for example, that equates to a family of four earning no more than $216,200 a year.

That down payment amount is based on the statewide median $900,000 price tag for a house, according to recent data from (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/sept2026sales) the California Assn. of Realtors. In Los Angeles County, the median price for a single-family home is $935,000. In Orange County, it’s $1.5 million.
Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households. For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state’s existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.

The ballot measure would allow qualified prospective homebuyers to borrow up to 17% of the sales price of a new home, contributing 3% of the down payment from their own funds.
The program would not be funded by taxpayers, but instead by the interest charged to borrowers on their down payment loans, also referred to as second mortgages. The measure has garnered widespread support, including from Gov. Gavin Newsom, statewide unions and mayors from Santa Monica to San José.
“Prop. 37 is a historic opportunity to expand homeownership opportunities for generations of working families — at zero cost or risk to taxpayers,” Newsom said in a statement.

But Proposition 37 carries a significant caveat: Any home purchased through the program must be new construction, which could limit its potential reach because of the high cost of building, some critics said.
Also, the proposition does not spell out the terms or interest rates on the loans, which would be worked out if the measure is approved. And some have questioned whether there will be sufficiently robust interest from investors to buy the state-issued bonds that will be used to fund the down payment loans.
The concept of down payment assistance is not new. Cities and states, including California, have long offered such programs to low- and middle-income homeowners, either in the form of loans or grants, and there are reportedly more than 2,700 such programs (https://downpaymentresource.com/professional-resource/down-payment-assistance-continues-to-expand-in-q1-2026-reaching-2679-programs-nationwide/) across the country.
Nevada, Connecticut, Massachusetts and New York all have programs to help homebuyers afford a down payment. Since 2021, New York has dispersed $70 million (https://www.ncsha.org/hfa-news/new-york-state-homes-and-community-renewal-announces-major-milestones-in-expanding-access-to-affordable-homeownership/) in down payment assistance. In Massachusetts, more than $146 million has been doled out in down payment help to homebuyers since 2020.
How the program would work
Under Proposition 37, down payment loans would work like any other, and would carry an interest rate and payback period — all of which would be determined by the California Housing Finance Agency.
To qualify, borrowers would need to have lived in the state for at least a year and earn no more than 200% of the local median income; in Los Angeles County, for example, that equates to a family of four earning no more than $216,200 a year.

Borrowers don’t have to be first-time homebuyers, which is often a requirement of down payment aid programs. But they would need to live in the home.

Prop 37 endorsement: Buying a home in California can feel impossible. Is this the fix?
Most down-payment assistance programs for home buyers drive up housing costs. Prop 37 is different.
S.F. Chronicle illustration from Getty Images elements
By Chronicle Editorial Board (https://www.sfchronicle.com/author/editorial-board/) , Opinion Staff Sep 15, 2026
It’s no secret that buying a home in California is a grim and mostly futile undertaking.
In the Bay Area, you need to make about $444,000 a year just to purchase a mid-priced home, according to a May report from the real estate brokerage Redfin (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/home-buy-income-bay-area-22281201.php). A 2025 Zillow study found (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/mortgage-rate-bay-area-20792146.php) that even if mortgage rates fell to 0%, most Bay Area families still couldn’t comfortably afford to buy.
Statewide, the median home price hovers around $900,000, according to the California Association of Realtors (https://carorg.sharepoint.com/:x:/s/CAR-RE-PublicProducts/IQAK-pU7cef4QpkWsCPlxwZKAbdKLa3OO0vFwHpuH_FADK8?rtime=9NSXc_YN30g). That puts a traditional 20% down payment out of reach for many families, locking them out of a pathway to generational wealth while simultaneously reducing the state’s political muscle as residents flee (https://www.ppic.org/blog/whos-leaving-california-and-whos-moving-in/) to cheaper, primarily red (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/editorials/article/housing-development-california-state-21027403.php), states.
Proposition 37 (https://vig.cdn.sos.ca.gov/2026/general/pdf/prop37-text-proposed-laws.pdf) on the November ballot promises to help solve these problems by making it easier for middle-class Californians to enter homeownership.

Article continues below this ad
The measure would permit the state to loan middle-income residents up to 17% of the cost of newly constructed houses, townhomes, row houses, condominiums and manufactured homes. Families with a traditional mortgage would only have to put 3% down.
Under Prop 37 in San Francisco, a family would need $40,000 for a median-priced home of about $1.3 million — compared to a 20% down payment of about $267,000.
Californians are clamoring for down payment help. When the state launched a down payment assistance program for first-time homebuyers in 2023, the $300 million on offer was spoken for in less than two weeks (https://www.sfchronicle.com/realestate/article/california-home-buyer-assistance-program-17888975.php).
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
But Prop 37 takes a different tack than traditional efforts like that one.
To start, it wouldn’t cost taxpayers a dime (https://lao.ca.gov/ballot/2026/prop37-110326.pdf).
The measure would authorize the California Housing Finance Agency to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds — which would be repaid by homeowners’ monthly loan and interest payments, not by taxpayers. Loan payments would also cover the administrative costs of the program, which will undergo an annual independent audit.
Nor will the measure drive up housing prices by subsidizing demand.
Only new homes explicitly constructed under the rules of the measure are eligible for Prop 37 loans. This incentivizes development instead of simply allowing more buyers to compete for a limited supply of existing homes.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Prop 37 aims to juice construction by eliminating red tape, particularly for condos.
Although condos are often the most affordable option for would-be homeowners, their production has fallen dramatically in California due to the state’s “right to repair” law, which effectively encourages homeowners to sue developers (https://www.sfchronicle.com/opinion/openforum/article/condo-home-california-law-22306098.php) for alleged construction defects — even easily fixable ones that aren’t harmful.
This year, Assembly Member Buffy Wicks, D-Oakland, attempted a fix with a bill (https://leginfo.legislature.ca.gov/faces/billTextClient.xhtml?bill_id=202520260AB1903) that would have comprehensively overhauled California’s right-to-repair law.
But it died in the final moments of the legislative session (https://calmatters.org/housing/2026/09/condo-construction-bill-dies/?utm_medium=email&utm_campaign=WhatMatters&utm_source=31&npnl=NTA2MTM0fDc4YTAyODgwNzMxZGY1NThiZTI5MGVlZGUxOTA2Y2VhYzNlNTFlMGM3YTJkYTNhNjZiNzFhZTljYzM1Njg5ODM&utm_source=ActiveCampaign&utm_medium=email&utm_content=Is%20Gavin%20Newsom%20in%20his%20lame%20duck%20era%3F&utm_campaign=WhatMatters) — even after being significantly watered down.
Prop 37 would reanimate some aspects of Wicks’ bill.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
It would require claimants to clearly specify each alleged violation and permit them to release builders from liability if repairs are completed satisfactorily. It also incentivizes quick resolution of lawsuits — builders could ask courts to dismiss actions against them if claimants drag their feet — and caps attorneys’ fees at 30% of total recovery.
With legislative reform in limbo, “the condo defect implications of Prop 37 are solid,” Leora Tanjuatco Ross, YIMBY Action’s California director, told the editorial board.
We certainly hope that lawmakers pursue more transformative defect reform in the future. But until that happens, Prop 37 could serve as a stopgap.
The ability of middle-class buyers to finance a home, such as these along Kirkwood Avenue in San Francisco, seen on April 9, 2022, would be enhanced with the passage of S.F.’s Prop 37 in November.
Justin Katigbak/For the S.F. Chronicle The measure also requires builders who want to take advantage of these right-to-repair reforms to meet certain labor standards, such as providing workers’ compensation and unemployment insurance, while abiding by state and local laws requiring prevailing wage — or union-level pay — for large-scale projects.
Advertisement
Article continues below this ad
Those who have lived in California for at least a year and have a family income of 80% to 200% of the area median income — which in San Francisco ranges from about $104,000 to $260,000 for a family of two (https://media.api.sf.gov/documents/2026_AMI-IncomeLimits-HMFA.pdf) — are eligible for Prop 37 loans.
No, you can’t use Prop 37 for a second home; qualifying homes must be the buyer’s primary residence. Eligible home prices are capped, too — they can’t be sold for more than 125% of the conforming loan limit for a one-unit property in the county in question, which is about $1.5 million in San Francisco.
The measure also contains consumer protections. For instance, it requires the program’s mortgage loans to be fixed-rate and instructs the California Housing Finance Agency to set them “as low as possible.” It also permits the agency to establish a homeowner education requirement.
Just how affordable these loans would be, however, is an open question. As a California Budget Center analysis noted (https://calbudgetcenter.org/resources/will-proposition-37-make-homeownership-more-affordable-its-not-guaranteed/#h-how-is-prop-37-different-from-california-s-existing-downpayment-assistance-programs), the Housing Finance Agency’s loans may come with higher-than-usual interest rates because they’re second mortgages. Investors view these as riskier than first mortgages, which are repaid first if a homeowner defaults.
Former state Sen. Bob Hertzberg, a Democrat from Los Angeles County who collected signatures to put Prop 37 on the ballot, told the editorial board that he believes the measure could create 190,000 homes and spur $150 billion in economic activity.
That certainly sounds transformative. But is the measure likely to live up to Hertzberg’s hype?
Prop 37 has no formal opposition and most experts we spoke with were cautiously supportive.
The measure technically didn’t need to go to the ballot; the Legislature or housing finance agency could have established the program. We’re not a fan of politicians using the ballot for their vanity projects, and there’s certainly some ego at play for Hertzberg, who referred to the homes that could be built under Prop 37 as “Hertzberg houses.”
But Hertzberg did try to get the Legislature to approve a version of the program (https://shou.senate.ca.gov/sites/shou.senate.ca.gov/files/7.%20SB%201457%20%28Hertzberg%29%20-%20analysis.pdf), to no avail.
“I’m just a burnt-out old politician trying to do the right thing who hasn’t lost his soul, and I might help the motherf—ers in the middle class if I die doing it,” said Hertzberg, who clearly subscribes to the John Burton school of profanity. (https://www.sfchronicle.com/politics/article/john-burton-obituary-17820175.php)

Prop 37’s scope is limited enough that we don’t think it will fundamentally change California’s housing landscape. But given how dire our housing crisis is, any positive impact is better than none at all.
We recommend a yes vote.

p]:text-cms-story-body-color-text" data-subscriber-content> Buying a home in California requires a colossal amount of money — and coming up with a 20% cash down payment of $180,000 for a median price home is a staggering hurdle for many would-be buyers.
That down payment amount is based on the statewide median $900,000 price tag for a house, according to recent data from (https://www.car.org/aboutus/mediacenter/newsreleases/2026releases/sept2026sales) the California Assn. of Realtors. Proposition 37 (https://www.latimes.com/california/story/2026-10-01/2026-california-election-proposition-37-loans-middle-class-homeowners-voter-guide) on the Nov. 3 ballot would allow the state to amass a $25 billion down payment assistance program for middle-class households. For perspective on the enormity of the measure before voters, one of the state’s existing down payment programs, California Dream For All, launched several years ago with $500 million, just 2% of the funding involved in Proposition 37.

# Your guide to Proposition 37: Loans for middle-income homeowners
Proposition 37 creates a program for middle-income families in California to borrow money to help buy a new home.
...
### What will the measure do?
The proposition creates a down payment loan program, totaling up to $25 billion, for middle-income families looking to buy a new home in California.
The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency, which already oversees several homeownership assistance programs.
The state would sell bonds to fund the program.
It would pay back investors using interest and loan payments from the program — not taxpayer money.
The California Housing Finance Agency would administer the program, including setting interest rates for the loans.
To qualify, prospective borrowers would need to buy a newly constructed home or a home that never has sold before, such as a commercial building that was converted into condos.

## What does California Proposition 37 do?
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos.
These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home.

The proposition creates a down payment loan program, totaling up to $25 billion, for middle-income families looking to buy a new home in California.
The program would be run by the California Housing Finance Agency, which already oversees several homeownership assistance programs.
The state would sell bonds to fund the program.

The California Housing Finance Agency would administer the program, including setting interest rates for the loans.

I'm pulling up the full Sacramento Bee editorial on Proposition 37, the same article syndicated across McClatchy papers, to see its reasoning. It calls the measure a mix of philanthropy, tort reform, housing construction, worker protection and Wall Street bond fees, which reads as a sharply critical take. Next I'm checking the KP angle.

I'm also checking the KPBS piece from October 2, since it lists arguments from some opponents. The Ballotpedia page returned only placeholder dots again, so I'm skipping it.

Be prepared for California’s midterms: Sign up for CalMatters' free election newsletter (https://calmatters.ac-page.com/california-elections-newsletter) and be the first to know when they update the CalMatters 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) with information on key races.
What does California Proposition 37 do?
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Supporter endorsements
California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)
Xavier Becerra (https://mailchi.mp/xavierbecerra2026/becerra-op-ed-they-created-a-crisis-in-la-to-cover-for-a-catastrophe-in-dc-13846143?e=dffea6c435)

California Conference of Carpenters (https://elections.cdn.sos.ca.gov/public-display/prop-37-arg-in-favor.pdf)
Opponents
Arguments against
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.
Opponent endorsements
Reform California (https://www.reformcalifornia.org/voter-guides/california)
League of Women Voters (https://lwvc.org/ballot-recommendations/)
Ballot text
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs.

This explainer was originally published by our news partners CalMatters. Be prepared for California’s midterms: Sign up for CalMatters' free election newsletter (https://calmatters.ac-page.com/california-elections-newsletter) and be the first to know when they update the CalMatters 2026 Voter Guide (https://calmatters.org/california-voter-guide-2026/) with information on key races.
What does California Proposition 37 do?
California’s Housing Finance Agency would be able (but not required) to borrow up to $25 billion to help would-be homebuyers purchase newly constructed houses and condos. These loans could provide up to 17% of a home’s purchase price, leaving buyers with a cash down payment of 3% if paired with a typical mortgage — $24,000 for an $800,000 home. Homebuyers would repay the loan in monthly installments to private lenders. Anyone earning up to twice the area’s median income would be eligible. Private lenders, not taxpayers, would be on the hook if homebuyers default. It was placed on the ballot by a coalition of real estate interests and labor unions.

What do supporters and opponents say?
Supporters
Arguments for
House hunters can expect to face a down payment equal to 20% of the value of a home. In California, where $700,000 for a fixer-upper is considered a steal in much of the state, that’s not feasible for most people. This loan program will put the dream of homeownership within reach of the middle class without costing taxpayers a dime.
Supporter endorsements
California Democratic Party (https://cadem.org/wp-content/uploads/2026/08/FINAL-2026-General-Election-Endorsements.pdf)
Xavier Becerra (https://mailchi.mp/xavierbecerra2026/becerra-op-ed-they-created-a-crisis-in-la-to-cover-for-a-catastrophe-in-dc-13846143?e=dffea6c435)

Opponents
Arguments against
Some opponents argue that state government should not be involved in the mortgage lending market and note that the measure won’t do much to address the underlying reasons that housing in California is so expensive. Others note that while it would help more people buy homes, it would only do so by allowing them to go into even deeper debt.
Opponent endorsements

Ballot text
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE. Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs.

I'm weighing whether to answer this ballot question with a bare yes or no, since it's a contested policy measure where the answer turns on values as much as facts. A one-word verdict would read as an objective call when it isn't, so I'm leaning toward laying out the considerations instead.

Proposition 37 on the November ballot is a peculiar mix of philanthropy, tort reform, housing construction, worker protection and Wall Street bond underwriting fees. Presented to voters as a solution to the lack of affordable homes for willing buyers, Prop. 37 aims to encourage developers to build “middle-class” housing and help “middle-class” families buy them without taxpayer assistance.
For builders, the program offers some protection from construction defect litigation and high attorney fees if they agree to be “qualified builders” (accepting liability for labor violations by contractors and subcontractors) and build “qualified new homes” (new construction or conversion with a price cap on each unit that does not exceed 125% of the conforming loan limit for that county, approximately $1 million to $1.5 million).
For buyers, the program offers fixed-rate second mortgages for 17% of the purchase price, no need for private mortgage insurance (PMI), and alternative “cash-flow underwriting” for buyers who otherwise might not qualify for a second mortgage. Borrowers are required to qualify for a first mortgage, and they must put down 3% of the purchase price from their own funds. To be eligible, borrowers must be California residents for at least one year and have a household income no higher than 200% of the area median income, adjusted for family size.
The program is financed with $25 billion in revenue bonds, issued by the state but repaid by adding the principal, interest and program administration costs to the payments made by the borrowers. Taxpayers have no direct risk.
The deceptive part of Proposition 37 is the representation, as stated in the ballot argument in favor of the measure, that “consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans.” Nothing in the measure guarantees that the second mortgages offered in the program will be less expensive for borrowers than loans available from private lenders.
The contention that the cost of the loans will be “below-market” rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%. These are revenue bonds, and the interest is not tax-free. In addition, they are not without risk. In the event of foreclosure, these second mortgages sit behind the first mortgages, with no back-up or guarantee from taxpayers.
That’s the part of the program that depends on philanthropy. The idea is that tax-exempt organizations will buy these bonds out of the goodness of their hearts and forgo the higher interest rates available from other bonds they could buy instead.
If that doesn’t happen, the California Housing Finance Agency will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates, potentially making the Prop. 37 second mortgage loans even more expensive for borrowers than loans offered by commercial lenders who don’t have to recoup the cost of administering this program.

Any developer can build price-capped “qualified new homes” eligible for the down payment assistance loans, but only “qualified builders” who accept the labor rules get the program’s protection from litigation and attorney fees. They lose the protection for an entire building, proponent Bob Hertzberg told our editorial board, if even one unit in it sells for above the capped price.
Home buyers should be aware that if a house or condominium sells for less than its fair market value, the county tax assessor will assess the property based on its fair market value, not on its purchase price.
Proposition 37 attempts to be a path through California’s minefield of regulations and liability in the housing sector, but it’s relying on the hope that non-profits will subsidize second mortgages so income-limited families who don’t have the money for a down payment can have two mortgage payments, not to mention the cost of homeowners insurance, HOA fees, property taxes and utility bills.

## Dual Tracking Prohibition in California
Dual tracking happens when a servicer simultaneously reviews a borrower for a loan modification or other foreclosure avoidance alternatives while at the same time going ahead with a foreclosure.
In the past, a lender or servicer could foreclose even while a loss mitigation application was pending.
The California Homeowner Bill of Rights prohibits the dual tracking of foreclosures in California.
Federal law also restricts dual tracking.
Under HBOR, if a borrower sends the servicer a complete application for a first lien loan modification at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, the servicer can't record a notice of default, notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale while the application is pending, and until:
- the servicer makes a written determination that the borrower isn't eligible for a first lien loan modification, and any appeal period has expired
- the borrower doesn't accept an offered first lien loan modification within 14 days of the offer, or
- the borrower accepts a written first lien loan modification but defaults on or otherwise breaches the borrower's obligations under the first lien loan modification.
(Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.6 (2025).)

## Dual Tracking Prohibition in California
Dual tracking happens when a servicer simultaneously reviews a borrower for a loan modification or other foreclosure avoidance alternatives while at the same time going ahead with a foreclosure.
In the past, a lender or servicer could foreclose even while a loss mitigation application was pending.
The California Homeowner Bill of Rights prohibits the dual tracking of foreclosures in California.
Federal law also restricts dual tracking.
Under HBOR, if a borrower sends the servicer a complete application for a first lien loan modification at least five business days before a scheduled foreclosure sale, the servicer can't record a notice of default, notice of sale, or conduct a trustee's sale while the application is pending, and until:
- the servicer makes a written determination that the borrower isn't eligible for a first lien loan modification, and any appeal period has expired
- the borrower doesn't accept an offered first lien loan modification within 14 days of the offer, or
- the borrower accepts a written first lien loan modification but defaults on or otherwise breaches the borrower's obligations under the first lien loan modification.
(Cal. Civ. Code § 2923.6 (2025).)

By The Editorial Board (https://www.dailynews.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 20, 2026 at 6:30 AM PDT

Proposition 37 on the November ballot is a peculiar mix of philanthropy, tort reform, housing construction, worker protection and Wall Street bond underwriting fees. Presented to voters as a solution to the lack of affordable homes for willing buyers, Prop. 37 aims to encourage developers to build “middle-class” housing and help “middle-class” families buy them without taxpayer assistance.
For builders, the program offers some protection from construction defect litigation and high attorney fees if they agree to be “qualified builders” (accepting liability for labor violations by contractors and subcontractors) and build “qualified new homes” (new construction or conversion with a price cap on each unit that does not exceed 125% of the conforming loan limit for that county, approximately $1 million to $1.5 million).
For buyers, the program offers fixed-rate second mortgages for 17% of the purchase price, no need for private mortgage insurance (PMI), and alternative “cash-flow underwriting” for buyers who otherwise might not qualify for a second mortgage. Borrowers are required to qualify for a first mortgage, and they must put down 3% of the purchase price from their own funds. To be eligible, borrowers must be California residents for at least one year and have a household income no higher than 200% of the area median income, adjusted for family size.
The program is financed with $25 billion in revenue bonds, issued by the state but repaid by adding the principal, interest and program administration costs to the payments made by the borrowers. Taxpayers have no direct risk.
The deceptive part of Proposition 37 is the representation, as stated in the ballot argument in favor of the measure, that “consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans.” Nothing in the measure guarantees that the second mortgages offered in the program will be less expensive for borrowers than loans available from private lenders.
The contention that the cost of the loans will be “below-market” rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%. These are revenue bonds, and the interest is not tax-free. In addition, they are not without risk. In the event of foreclosure, these second mortgages sit behind the first mortgages, with no back-up or guarantee from taxpayers.
That’s the part of the program that depends on philanthropy. The idea is that tax-exempt organizations will buy these bonds out of the goodness of their hearts and forgo the higher interest rates available from other bonds they could buy instead.
If that doesn’t happen, the California Housing Finance Agency will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates, potentially making the Prop. 37 second mortgage loans even more expensive for borrowers than loans offered by commercial lenders who don’t have to recoup the cost of administering this program.

Any developer can build price-capped “qualified new homes” eligible for the down payment assistance loans, but only “qualified builders” who accept the labor rules get the program’s protection from litigation and attorney fees. They lose the protection for an entire building, proponent Bob Hertzberg told our editorial board, if even one unit in it sells for above the capped price.
Home buyers should be aware that if a house or condominium sells for less than its fair market value, the county tax assessor will assess the property based on its fair market value, not on its purchase price.
Proposition 37 attempts to be a path through California’s minefield of regulations and liability in the housing sector, but it’s relying on the hope that non-profits will subsidize second mortgages so income-limited families who don’t have the money for a down payment can have two mortgage payments, not to mention the cost of homeowners insurance, HOA fees, property taxes and utility bills.
It sounds to us like it won’t have a good outcome. Vote no on Proposition 37.

Borrowers are required to qualify for a first mortgage, and they must put down 3% of the purchase price from their own funds. To be eligible, borrowers must be California residents for at least one year and have a household income no higher than 200% of the area median income, adjusted for family size.
The program is financed with $25 billion in revenue bonds, issued by the state but repaid by adding the principal, interest and program administration costs to the payments made by the borrowers. Taxpayers have no direct risk.
The deceptive part of Proposition 37 is the representation, as stated in the ballot argument in favor of the measure, that “consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans.” Nothing in the measure guarantees that the second mortgages offered in the program will be less expensive for borrowers than loans available from private lenders.
The contention that the cost of the loans will be “below-market” rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%. These are revenue bonds, and the interest is not tax-free. In addition, they are not without risk. In the event of foreclosure, these second mortgages sit behind the first mortgages, with no back-up or guarantee from taxpayers.
That’s the part of the program that depends on philanthropy. The idea is that tax-exempt organizations will buy these bonds out of the goodness of their hearts and forgo the higher interest rates available from other bonds they could buy instead.
If that doesn’t happen, the California Housing Finance Agency will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates, potentially making the Prop. 37 second mortgage loans even more expensive for borrowers than loans offered by commercial lenders who don’t have to recoup the cost of administering this program.

Dual tracking happens when a servicer simultaneously reviews a borrower for a loan modification or other foreclosure avoidance alternatives while at the same time going ahead with a foreclosure.

By The Editorial Board (https://www.dailynews.com/author/the-editorial-board/) | opinion@scng.com (mailto:opinion@scng.com)
PUBLISHED: September 20, 2026 at 6:30 AM PDT

Proposition 37 on the November ballot is a peculiar mix of philanthropy, tort reform, housing construction, worker protection and Wall Street bond underwriting fees. Presented to voters as a solution to the lack of affordable homes for willing buyers, Prop. 37 aims to encourage developers to build “middle-class” housing and help “middle-class” families buy them without taxpayer assistance.
For builders, the program offers some protection from construction defect litigation and high attorney fees if they agree to be “qualified builders” (accepting liability for labor violations by contractors and subcontractors) and build “qualified new homes” (new construction or conversion with a price cap on each unit that does not exceed 125% of the conforming loan limit for that county, approximately $1 million to $1.5 million).
For buyers, the program offers fixed-rate second mortgages for 17% of the purchase price, no need for private mortgage insurance (PMI), and alternative “cash-flow underwriting” for buyers who otherwise might not qualify for a second mortgage. Borrowers are required to qualify for a first mortgage, and they must put down 3% of the purchase price from their own funds. To be eligible, borrowers must be California residents for at least one year and have a household income no higher than 200% of the area median income, adjusted for family size.
The program is financed with $25 billion in revenue bonds, issued by the state but repaid by adding the principal, interest and program administration costs to the payments made by the borrowers. Taxpayers have no direct risk.
The deceptive part of Proposition 37 is the representation, as stated in the ballot argument in favor of the measure, that “consumer benefits include below-market, fixed-rate loans.” Nothing in the measure guarantees that the second mortgages offered in the program will be less expensive for borrowers than loans available from private lenders.
The contention that the cost of the loans will be “below-market” rests on the assumption that foundations and non-profits will be willing to buy the bonds at a below-market interest rate of 3%. These are revenue bonds, and the interest is not tax-free. In addition, they are not without risk. In the event of foreclosure, these second mortgages sit behind the first mortgages, with no back-up or guarantee from taxpayers.
That’s the part of the program that depends on philanthropy. The idea is that tax-exempt organizations will buy these bonds out of the goodness of their hearts and forgo the higher interest rates available from other bonds they could buy instead.
If that doesn’t happen, the California Housing Finance Agency will sell the bonds in the market and pay market interest rates, potentially making the Prop. 37 second mortgage loans even more expensive for borrowers than loans offered by commercial lenders who don’t have to recoup the cost of administering this program.

Any developer can build price-capped “qualified new homes” eligible for the down payment assistance loans, but only “qualified builders” who accept the labor rules get the program’s protection from litigation and attorney fees. They lose the protection for an entire building, proponent Bob Hertzberg told our editorial board, if even one unit in it sells for above the capped price.
Home buyers should be aware that if a house or condominium sells for less than its fair market value, the county tax assessor will assess the property based on its fair market value, not on its purchase price.
Proposition 37 attempts to be a path through California’s minefield of regulations and liability in the housing sector, but it’s relying on the hope that non-profits will subsidize second mortgages so income-limited families who don’t have the money for a down payment can have two mortgage payments, not to mention the cost of homeowners insurance, HOA fees, property taxes and utility bills.
It sounds to us like it won’t have a good outcome. Vote no on Proposition 37.

(a) As used in this section:
(1) “Borrower” has the same meaning as defined in Section 2929.5.
(2) “Mortgage servicer” includes the current mortgage servicer and any prior mortgage servicers.
(3) “Subordinate mortgage” means a security instrument in residential real property, including a deed of trust and any security instrument that functions in the form of a mortgage, that was, at the time it was recorded, subordinate to another security interest encumbering the same residential real property.
(b) The following conduct constitutes an unlawful practice
in connection with a subordinate mortgage:
(1) The mortgage servicer did not provide the borrower with any written communication regarding the loan secured by the mortgage for at least three years.
(2) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan servicing notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Real Estate Settlement Procedures Act, as amended (12 U.S.C. Sec. 2601 et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(3) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a transfer of loan ownership notice to the borrower when required to provide that notice by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(4) The mortgage servicer conducted or threatened to conduct a foreclosure sale after providing a form to the borrower indicating that the debt had been written off or discharged, including, but not limited to, an Internal Revenue Service Form 1099.
(5) The mortgage servicer conducted or threatened to conduct a foreclosure sale after the applicable statute of limitations expired.
(6) The mortgage servicer failed to provide a periodic account statement to the borrower when required to provide that statement by law, including, but not limited to, the federal Truth in Lending Act, as amended (15 U.S.C. 1601, et seq.), and investor or guarantor requirements.
(c) A mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent shall not conduct or
threaten to conduct a nonjudicial foreclosure until the mortgage servicer, mortgagee, trustee, beneficiary, or authorized agent does both of the following:
(1) Simultaneously with the recording of a notice of default, records or causes to be recorded, in the office of the county recorder of the county that the encumbered property is located, a certification under penalty of perjury that either:
(A) The mortgage servicer did not engage in an unlawful practice as described in subdivision (b).
(B) The mortgage servicer lists all instances when it committed an unlawful practice as described in subdivision (b).
(2) Simultaneously with the service of a recorded notice of default, sends both of the following documents to the borrower by United States certified
mail with return receipt requested to the last known mailing address of the borrower:
(A) A notice providing that if the borrower believes the mortgage servicer engaged in an unlawful practice described in subdivision (b) or misrepresented its compliance history, the borrower may petition the court for relief before the foreclosure sale.
(B) A copy of the certification recorded pursuant to paragraph (1).
(d) Upon a borrower’s petition to the court for relief before the foreclosure sale, the court shall enjoin a proposed foreclosure sale pursuant to a power of sale in a subordinate mortgage until a final determination on the petition has been made.
(e) It shall be an affirmative defense in a judicial foreclosure proceeding if the court finds the mortgage
servicer engaged in any of the unlawful practices specified in subdivision (b).
(f) The court may provide equitable remedies that the court deems appropriate, depending on the extent and severity of the mortgage servicer’s violations. The equitable remedies may include, but are not limited to, striking all or a portion of the arrears claim, barring foreclosure, or permitting foreclosure subject to future compliance and corrected arrearage claim.
(g) A borrower may also petition the court to set a nonjudicial foreclosure sale aside when a certification required by subdivision (c) was never recorded or when a certification recorded pursuant to subdivision (c) indicates that the mortgage servicer engaged in an unlawful practice described in subdivision (b) or misrepresented its compliance history.
(h) Any failure to
comply with the provisions of this section shall not affect the validity of a trustee’s sale or a sale in favor of a bona fide purchaser.
(Added by Stats. 2025, Ch. 22, Sec. 2. (AB 130) Effective June 30, 2025.)

I'm noting that Civil Code 2924.13, added by AB 130 in 2025, gives protections to borrowers with subordinate mortgages: it bars foreclosure sales once the statute of limitations has run or the debt is written off, requires certification before a nonjudicial foreclosure, and lets borrowers petition a court to enjoin such a sale. Now I'm checking how Prop 37 refers to that same section.

I'm checking the exact wording Prop 37 uses to exempt middle-class home ownership loans from that section, since it would take those second mortgages out of the borrower protections it provides.

I'm noting that the exemption would take second mortgages out of a 2025 state law that adds protections against certain foreclosure practices on those loans, like certification before a nonjudicial sale and the right to ask a court to halt one. The program's own consumer protections, such as fixed rates, capped origination fees, and no prepayment penalty, are likely to be the Yes side's counterpoint. I also want to confirm that the state general fund isn't on the hook, since the LAO found no direct state or local costs.

I'm weighing a few claims about Prop 37's cost and risk. The Yes side says there's zero cost to taxpayers, and the LAO agrees on direct costs, though critics like Hoover argue there's contingent risk. The "190,000 homes" projection came from the Yes campaign itself, and the author concedes it's at the high end. The "below-market" language appears in the ballot argument but the measure only says "to the greatest extent possible," so it isn't guaranteed.

I'm weighing how to frame the answer: a one-word yes or no won't work here since this is a values question on a contested measure, so I'll lay out the key facts and what the decision hinges on. I'm also considering whether to offer a tentative view, but I'm leaning toward staying neutral and instead inviting the user to share their priorities so I can help them map those to a vote.

Now I'm drafting the answer: a clear note that a one-word yes or no won't fit this values question, then a short summary of what Prop 37 does, and an offer to map the user's priorities onto the facts.

Now I'm weighing the case for yes: the program doesn't draw on the state general fund, and the bonds are repaid by borrowers, so investors rather than taxpayers would absorb losses. It also goes after the down payment, which is often the real barrier, and it ties aid to new construction with an optional path for builders to limit some defect lawsuits. Backers include Newsom, the state Democratic Party, and others.

I'm weighing the case against the measure now: the rate, term, and monthly payment aren't set until after a vote, and riskier second mortgages could push investors toward high rates, so a $136,000 loan at 7% would run about $900 a month. Nothing guarantees the "below-market" rates either, since they depend on philanthropic buyers at around 3%, and I'm also weighing whether limiting aid to new homes adds supply or just bids up prices.

I won't give a one-word yes or no on this one. Whether yes or no is better depends on how you weigh real down-payment help against a second monthly loan and some unresolved risks, and informed people land on both sides. I reviewed the official guide, the LAO analysis, the measure text, PPIC and CalMatters analyses, and the major editorial positions. Here's what matters most.

**What it does**
- Lets the state sell up to $25 billion in bonds to fund second mortgages covering up to 17% of a new home's price. Buyers still put 3% down, earn up to 200% of area median income, and repay the second loan monthly.
- The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost, since borrowers repay the bonds. The measure says the bonds are not state debt.

**Case for yes**
- It targets the down payment, often the real barrier. PPIC found about 90% of renters would meet the income limit.
- It covers only newly built homes and gives builders a path to fewer defect lawsuits, aiming to add supply.
- Backers include Gov. Newsom, the California Democratic Party, the Realtors, carpenters' unions, and the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board.

**Case for no**
- The rate, term, and monthly payment are set after the vote. Second mortgages are riskier for investors, so rates could be high. At 7% over 30 years, a $136,000 loan is about $900 a month.
- "Below-market" is not guaranteed. It depends partly on foundations buying bonds at about 3%. Otherwise the bonds would sell at market rates.
- PPIC estimates that, in 2024 and before any second loan, 56% of renters couldn't afford an entry-level new home under a 36% debt-to-income limit.
- Limiting aid to new homes may not add enough supply and could push prices up. The LAO lists investor demand, loan costs, and whether construction actually rises as open questions.
- Builders who opt in get a modified defect-repair process, including a path to dismissal if homeowners stall, in exchange for accepting liability for contractors' labor violations. The measure also caps attorney contingency fees in defect suits at 30% (courts can approve more). It exempts these loans from Civil Code § 2924.13, a 2025 law that adds protections for second-mortgage borrowers facing foreclosure.
- The League of Women Voters, the San Diego Union-Tribune, and the Southern California News Group and East Bay Times editorial boards oppose it. No opposing committee has reported money. The Yes side has raised more than $30 million, mostly from Realtors.

**How to decide**
- Yes fits if you can afford a second monthly payment, think the program will add homes rather than raise prices, and accept the builder-liability changes.
- No fits if the monthly cost and unknown terms worry you, you doubt the supply effect, or you prefer targeted programs like CalHFA's existing loans, which defer repayment but have tighter eligibility.

If you tell me which of these matters most to you, I can point to the specific evidence on it.

I won't give a one-word yes or no on this one. Whether yes or no is better depends on how you weigh real down-payment help against a second monthly loan and some unresolved risks, and informed people land on both sides. I reviewed the official guide, the LAO analysis, the measure text, PPIC and CalMatters analyses, and the major editorial positions. Here's what matters most.

**What it does**
- Lets the state sell up to $25 billion in bonds to fund second mortgages covering up to 17% of a new home's price. Buyers still put 3% down, earn up to 200% of area median income, and repay the second loan monthly.
- The Legislative Analyst finds no direct state or local cost, since borrowers repay the bonds. The measure says the bonds are not state debt.

**Case for yes**
- It targets the down payment, often the real barrier. PPIC found about 90% of renters would meet the income limit.
- It covers only newly built homes and gives builders a path to fewer defect lawsuits, aiming to add supply.
- Backers include Gov. Newsom, the California Democratic Party, the Realtors, carpenters' unions, and the San Francisco Chronicle's editorial board.

**Case for no**
- The rate, term, and monthly payment are set after the vote. Second mortgages are riskier for investors, so rates could be high. At 7% over 30 years, a $136,000 loan is about $900 a month.
- "Below-market" is not guaranteed. It depends partly on foundations buying bonds at about 3%. Otherwise the bonds would sell at market rates.
- PPIC estimates that, in 2024 and before any second loan, 56% of renters couldn't afford an entry-level new home under a 36% debt-to-income limit.
- Limiting aid to new homes may not add enough supply and could push prices up. The LAO lists investor demand, loan costs, and whether construction actually rises as open questions.
- Builders who opt in get a modified defect-repair process, including a path to dismissal if homeowners stall, in exchange for accepting liability for contractors' labor violations. The measure also caps attorney contingency fees in defect suits at 30% (courts can approve more). It exempts these loans from Civil Code § 2924.13, a 2025 law that adds protections for second-mortgage borrowers facing foreclosure.
- The League of Women Voters, the San Diego Union-Tribune, and the Southern California News Group and East Bay Times editorial boards oppose it. No opposing committee has reported money. The Yes side has raised more than $30 million, mostly from Realtors.

**How to decide**
- Yes fits if you can afford a second monthly payment, think the program will add homes rather than raise prices, and accept the builder-liability changes.
- No fits if the monthly cost and unknown terms worry you, you doubt the supply effect, or you prefer targeted programs like CalHFA's existing loans, which defer repayment but have tighter eligibility.

If you tell me which of these matters most to you, I can point to the specific evidence on it.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
SUMMARY
Put on the Ballot by Petition Signatures
Authorizes $25 billion in bonds to offer eligible buyers fixed-rate mortgages for up to 17% of purchase price of a newly constructed home priced below about $1.5 million. Borrowers must be California residents, occupy the home, meet income limits, and pay at least 3% down. Bonds repaid by mortgage payments, not State. Fiscal Impact: No direct state or local costs. Supporters: United Nurses Associations of California; California Conference of Carpenters; California State Treasurer Fiona Ma Opponents: None submitted
WHAT YOUR VOTE MEANS
YES
A YES vote on this measure means: The state would create a new homebuying assistance program. The state could sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds to fund the program. Bonds would be paid back by homeowners’ payments on their home loans.
NO
A NO vote on this measure means: The state would not be required to create a new homebuying assistance program.
ARGUMENTS
PRO
Zero Taxpayer Cost-No Taxpayer Risk. Prop. 37 makes buying a home more affordable, keeping homeownership attainable for hardworking and middle-class Californians, with low-interest mortgages funded by private bond investors, NOT TAXPAYERS. Must be CA resident to qualify, meet income requirements, occupy home, make monthly payments, repay loan. Strict accountability/audits.
CON
NO ARGUMENT AGAINST PROPOSITION 37 WAS SUBMITTED.

PROP
37
CREATES LOAN PROGRAM FOR MIDDLE-INCOME BUYERS OF QUALIFIED NEW HOMES. INITIATIVE STATUTE.
ANALYSIS BY THE LEGISLATIVE ANALYST
BACKGROUND
State Revenue Bonds. Bonds are a way that governments borrow money, most commonly for public projects such as schools or bridges. The state sells bonds to investors to receive up-front funding for these projects. Over time, investors are repaid with interest. The state sells two main types of bonds: general obligation bonds and revenue bonds. The state usually repays general obligation bonds using the state General Fund. (The General Fund is the account the state uses to pay for most public services, including education, health care, and prisons.) In contrast, revenue bonds are repaid using revenue from fees or other payments by the users of the project (such as from bridge tolls).
Some People Seek Down Payment Assistance. When purchasing a home, most people pay some of the cost up front-typically 3 percent to 20 percent of the home price. The up-front payment is known as a down payment. If people cannot afford the down payment, there are different government programs available to provide down payment assistance to eligible homebuyers. To cover the remaining cost of the home, homebuyers get a loan, called a mortgage. Homebuyers then pay off the mortgage by making monthly payments that include interest.
California Housing Finance Agency (CalHFA). CalHFA is a state entity that administers programs designed to help low- and moderate-income Californians afford housing. CalHFA has a few programs that provide down payment assistance to homebuyers. The down payment assistance programs are loans that must be repaid under certain terms and conditions.
Construction Defect Law. To try to prevent construction defects, state law sets minimum standards that builders must follow for new residential construction. Current law also establishes a process that homeowners and housing builders must follow before a homeowner is able to sue a builder for alleged violations of those minimum standards. For example, the homeowner must provide notice to the builder that includes certain information concerning a claim of construction defect.
PROPOSAL
Revenue Bond to Pay for a New Down Payment Assistance Program. Proposition 37 allows CalHFA to sell up to $25 billion in revenue bonds. CalHFA would use the bond funds to create a down payment assistance program called the “middle-class homeownership loan.” Each loan would cover up to 17 percent of the home price. (Homebuyers would need to provide a down payment of at least 3 percent of the home price.) Homeowners’ monthly payments on their loan would be designed to repay the bonds over time and cover the program’s administrative costs. CalHFA also would be required to keep interest costs for homebuyers as low as possible. CalHFA would decide how much of the bonds to issue (up to $25 billion) and over what time period.
Buyers and Homes Must Meet Certain Requirements. To participate in a middleclass homeownership loan, people and homes would need to meet certain requirements. For example, an applicant would need to be a resident of the state and have a household income no more than double the typical income level in their area. For a home to be eligible for purchase through the program, among other requirements, the buyer would need to be the first purchaser of the home and the price could not exceed certain limits.
Housing Developer Options. Under Proposition 37, all developers could build homes eligible for purchase under the program. Developers also could choose to participate in a “qualified builder option.” Developers that chose this option would be required to meet higher labor standards, such as using workers with a certain type of training for certain types of housing projects. In exchange, developers would be subject to different construction defect rules, which generally aim to provide more flexibility to developers.
FISCAL EFFECTS
No Direct State or Local Costs. Because Proposition 37 uses the payments from homebuyers to repay bond investors, it would not result in direct state or local costs.
Other Potential Effects. A number of factors, which are unknown at this time, could affect Proposition 37’s scope and impact. These include (1) the extent to which investors want to buy the bond, (2) how much the loans available under this proposed program cost homebuyers compared with other down payment assistance options, and (3) whether the program results in increased home construction and homebuying.
